To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
trauma-induced suppressive active peptide can cause significant T-cell changes predictive of septic shock.
the suppressive peptide is an important component of the post-trauma immunosuspersion.
trauma patients who develop sepsis have a significant decrease in total T-cells and helper cells, and a significant increase in activated T-cells and IL-2 expressing T-cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
identifying changes in the immune system which occur following trauma and which may be predictive of the development of clinical sepsis in trauma patients.
the identification of the mechanisms of trauma-induced immunosuppressive changes.
the role of lymphocyte changes and the presence or absence of a low molecular peptide in the development of sepsis following severe trauma.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the suppressive active peptides found following trauma may be responsible for some but not all of the T-cell changes predictive of septic complications.
trauma-induced suppressive peptide can cause changes in T-cell antigen expression which are similar to changes seen in patients developing sepsis.
the suppressive peptide can induce changes in lymphocytes which are similar to those found in patients who develop sepsis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the suppressive active peptides can be used to predict the development of sepsis and can be used to explain the immunosuppression seen following trauma.
the suppressive active peptides found in trauma patients who develop sepsis are capable of inducing changes in T-cell antigens which are also seen in patients who develop septic complications.
post-trauma T-cells changes predictive of septic shock are induced by trauma and not by trauma-induced suppressive peptide.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the suppressive peptide may have a role in immunosuppression and that the changes in the T cell subpopulations that occur in patients that develop sepsis may be related to the presence of the suppressive peptide.

trauma causes a shift in T-cell subpopulations and expression of differentiation antigens, which are predictive of sepsisis, and these changes can be reproduced by incubation of suppressive active peptide and normal lymphocytes.
we have found a new way to identify patients at risk of infection and death.
